" Call his name ! Let Walyarima

Be our signal cry ;
Ye who seek emancipation
From your husbands' domination,

Now behold it nigh ! "

II.

But three men saw Walyarima

From a neighbouring wood,
Saw and heard, and told the story —
Told their chief, " To-eyborori," »

How the matter stood.

To the women, on the morrow,

Calm, the chieftain said,
" Toilsome hunting is before us,
Hunger may be hanging o'er us :

Make cassava bread."

When for roots they all departed,

To the stream he went ;
Bade some striplings there " keep moving,"
While, concealed, the rest (approving)

Heard his stern intent.

Those who bathed cried, " Walyarima ! " —

Called the hated name,
Spread their long hair on the water ;

1 "Walyarima" is the name of the animal whose appearance was
assumed by the lover while swimming the river. To-eyborori" and
"To-eyza" are titles, denoting authority, masculine and feminine
respectively. The proper names seem to have been lost in the lapse of
jears.

1 82 LEGENDS AND MYTHS OF THE

While each bow lay near for slaughter ;
Walyarima came.

As he came, the chief, to meet him,

Dashed into the tide,
Sent his mighty arrow through him ;
While the others, swimming to him,

Smote him — as he died.

Grimly, his remains they bore then

To the women's shed —
To the ridge within, suspended,
Left them (for a taunt intended)

Hanging overhead.

Came, in Indian file, the women :

Each her burden bore ;
Sternly then their husbands eyed them,
Shrinking from the sights beside them,

On the roof and floor.

Last of all came in To-eyza :

Blood fell on her hand,
Firm she stood, her high head rearing
(E'en the chief admired her bearing)

Beautiful and grand !

Then said he, " We go a-hunting ;

Speed, and make the bread —
Bake to-night : we cannot tarry,
Bread for five days we must carry."

" Be it so,'' she said."
}

" Bring the meat ; and strong paiwdri,

More than e'er before ;
We your wives will then provide you,
And, that night, will dance beside you,

If we dance no more ! "

III.

In the heart of proud To-eyza

Burned a raging flame ;
For that drop of blood inspired her,
And the demon power, which fired her.

On the others came.

" For revenge our hearts are burning —

All our hearts,'' said she.
" Savage insult men provide you !
Ask no questions — I will guide you ;

You shall all be free ! "

* * * :|: *

From his hunting came the chieftain ;

Laden were his men.
Beasts and birds they brought home twenty,
Smoked or fresh. Then all was plenty —

All was feasting then !

For the women of paiwari

Had abundant store —
All the men had drunk, and rested ;
Till the thirsty ones requested

To be served with more.

Then a calabash each woman
Filled up to the brim,

1 84 LEGENDS AND MYTHS OF THE

To her husband meekly handed,
(So To-eyza had commanded)
Fatal draught to him !

She had mixed cassava juice there,

Bringing death to all ;
Soon, in agony appalling,
Vainly for assistance calling,

Down the warriors fall.

" Now rejoice ! " exclaimed To-eyza ;

" Women, ye are free !
Nevermore shall husbands rule you,
Beat, oppress, and then befool you,

If you follow me ! "

Some, with boys, had fled ; the others
Through the midnight hour

Danced, with simulated gladness ;

Every bosom filled with madness,
By the demon's power !

IV.

Winding through the woods in order,

See a female band,
Hammocks, food, and weapons bearing,
lor a weary march preparing,

To some distant land."
}

To their leader, tall To-eyza,

All obedience pay. —
Sometimes fighting, sometimes flying,
Mainly on their bows relying,

They must win their way.

Many a discontented woman

With them gladly goes.
They proclaim emancipation ;
Call themselves the " Woman's nation ; "

Husbands treat as foes.

Driving off the men, or slaying,

To their wives they say,
" With your daughters we receive you ;
If you keep your sons, we leave you

Here, with them to stay."

On they march, and others follow,

Swelling thus their band;
O'er those females madness creeping ;
Like an epidemic, sweeping

Women from the land.
* * * * *
But, meanwhile, the poisoned victims

Kindly friends had found ;
Shuddered at the bones before them,
Scared the vultures brooding o'er them ;

Placed them in the ground.

Then they followed up those women,

Made the hindmost fly ;
Swiftly chased to overtake them,
But their captives none could make them,

They preferred to die.

Soon they came to dark green forests,

Saw their bravest fall ;
In their blood the strong men weltered,
Shot by female archers, sheltered

By each leafy wall.

Then they paused ; a wise man saying,

" What have we to gain ?
Of what use to man is woman,
Who regards him as a foeman ?

Let them march again ! "

So those women, still proceeding

Towards the setting sun,
Passing safely through all dangers,
Made a settlement as strangers,

All their journeys done.

There their haughty queen, To-eyza,
Gave them maxims clear :
• " We will welcome men as lovers,

None must settle here.

" Of their children born amongst us,

  "passage_text": "ABORIGINAL TRIBES OF GUIANA. 191

LEGEND OF SERIKOAI.
I.

In days when spirits talked with men,

And all the world was young,
Wawaiya, lately made a bride,
Saw a young tapir by her side

Walk quietly along.

" Oh, what art thou," the woman said,

" Thus walking here by me ? "
" They call me ' Wailya,' " he replied,
" With changed form I seek thy side,

For thou art fair to see ! "

She, when her husband went to hunt,

Would to their field repair ;
And daily, as she went and came,
Through forest path, it was the same —

She met the tapir there.

And pleasantly the creature spoke,

And well she loved to hear ;
Till, through his artful, glozing word,
Serikoai, her once-loved lord,

Became to her less dear.

Then boldly the seducer said,

" Come, run away with me !
Tar, far away we both will fly,
And, where this wide earth meets the sky,

My country thou shalt see.

192 LEGENDS AND MYTHS OF THE

" 'Tis there I reign in manly form :
There thou shalt be my bride ! "
" Alas ! " she cried, " if I should fly,
My husband, brave Serikoai,
Would slay us side by side ! "

"I charm thine axe," the sorcerer said,

" And it shall speak to thee.
Heed well what that good axe shall say,
And see thou do it. That same day
Thou shalt be safe with me!"

II.

" Wawaiya," said Serikoai,

" Come where our pear-trees grow.
In yonder old provision ground
Last month I saw young fruits abound ;

They must be ripe, I know."

" I go with thee," the wife replied,

" But I mine axe must take.
Whilst thou art climbing in the tree,
I'll cut such dry wood as I see,

Our nightly fire to make."

Then to the sharp'ning stone she went,

As if her axe to grind ;
And every time it touched the stone,
The word " Sahtai," in threatening tone,

Seemed borne upon the wind."
}

" Dost thou not hear, Serikoai,

The axe here speak to me ?
Still, as I rub, these words resound,
Oh ! ' I must cut ; ' or, 'I must wound !'

What can their meaning be ? "

" Whene'er an axe is sharpened there,"
Said he, " I hear the same ;

So let us haste, nor lose the day,

To idle fancies giving way ;
Women are oft to blame."

Resentment then within her burned,

As with her lord she went.
That direful sorcerer drew her on,
And with his charms her heart had gone,

Till she could not repent.

Then many ripening fruits they saw,

Bananas sweet were there ;
But still the man would climb that tree,
Where he his fav'rite fruit could see,

The " avocado " pear.

Wawaiya, cast thine axe away,

Bid the enchanter flee !
Why do thy handsome features frown ?
Slay not thy husband coming down ;

For good and true is he !
14

194 LEGENDS AND MYTHS OF THE

Alas ! — inspired by direful charm,

(The axe its influence knew,)
She raised her hands to strike the blow,
The deed is done — the man lies low,
His leg is clean cut through !

She meets his eye, and in it reads

Wonder and deepest woe !
Then hurries from that bloody scene :
With Wailya, through the forests green,
And o'er the hills to go.

III.

The husband lay, and thought to die ;
• His life-blood ebbed away.
A kindly spirit passing then —
A friend to true and suffering men —
Revived him as he lay.

Inspired, the man an eyelash plucked,

(Upon it was a tear ;)
He blew it in the air — it flew,
A little bird of beauteous hue ;

Then waited, hovering near.

" O birdie !" said the bleeding man,

" Haste ! to my mother fly,
And call my name ! " The birdie knew,
And straightway to the mother flew.;

And called, " Serikoai ! ""
}

" Why call my son, ' Serikoai ? '

Oh, birdie, tell me true !
Why dost thou nutter to and fro ?
Thy meaning, bird, I cannot know."

Then back the sweet bird flew —

And swiftly came again the bird,
Taught by the suff'ring man :
" Oh, mother ! thy Serikoai
Is sorely wounded — left to die ! "■
Forthwith the mother ran ;

She ran, and stumbled as she ran,

(Old age asserts its power) ;
Yet through dense bush she hurried on,
To help her foully-stricken son
In that malignant hour.

" Oh, loving mother ! art thou come

Thy dying son to cheer ?
Better than all fair wives, like mine,
To whom fond men their hearts resign,

Is one good mother near ! "

Then that kind spirit saw their love,

Propitious from on high :
To healing balsams added charms,
Till, saved, in his good mother's arms

He left Serikoai.

196 LEGENDS AND MYTHS.

IV.

Oh, who is this that wanders on,

Still searching all the ground ?
A man of mighty strength he seems ;
Though pale and worn ; — his keen eye gleams

On everything around.

A wooden prop one limb supports

The shapely leg is gone !
Yet, like a warrior armed for fight,
With bow and club from morn till night,

He still keeps moving on.

And every forest path he tries,

No track there meets his eye.
For many an eve, and many a dawn,
Have passed since that false wife has gone

Who maimed Serikoai.

The rains, which washed her track away,

Had left no traces near ;
No sign where human life had been :
Till, near some trees, a sprout was seen

Of avocado pear.

He scanned the bush all round, and thought

An opening he could spy ;
And followed that until he found,
Another pear-shoot on the ground ;

Then brighter shone his eye.

' With bow and club, from morn till night,
He still keeps moving on.""

" Some people of old

(So our forefathers told)
Had their village above the great fall.

One, a feeble old man,

Passing life's usual span,
Was half blind, and a burden to all.

" For, though once strong and fleet,

His poor suffering feet
(It might happen to white men or negroes,

For want of due care)

Had — burrowing there —
Some scores of vile vermin, called "chegoes."

(Some ladies, we've heard,

Take offence at that word,

And express it with more or less vigour.

ABORIGINAL TRIBES OF GUIANA. 203

We would give no offence,
So, in the same sense,
Will use " insect," and banish the-

The old man grew more helpless, and gave them more

work,
And the care of his feet more and more they would shirk ;

Till the young women all,

And the boys, great and small,
Said, " Oh ! what is the use ? Let him lie there and bawl !
His feet every day are becoming more sore,
As the insects increase there each day more and more ;
We give up the care of him ! Mind him, who can ?
He's become such a troublesome, horrid old man ! "

What was to be done ? Though they all wished him dead,

The men were unwilling to cleave his poor head.

" Let him go to the spirit-land ! " some then would say,

" The river may take him and bear him away,

If he still suffer here he must die all the same !

We can help him no more, so we are not to blame."

Then the head men commanded, " Bring now a wood-skin ;
Put the old man and his little property in ;

Let nothing remain,

For we seek no such gain,
But to get rid of trouble and finish his pain.
So we send him away the next world to begin,
But will not send him empty, for that were a sin."

204 LEGENDS AND MYTHS OF THE

The young men obeyed. They soon brought a wood-skin,

Put the old man and his little property in ;

They then launched him forth. As he swept down the

stream,
The loud-growing roar must have seemed a bad dream ;
One quivering moment — then, over the fall
Went wood-skin and victim, with " insects " and all !

Perhaps just then his countrymen

Felt they had not done well ;
And the bell-bird bright in plumage white

Tolled forth his passing knell.

It may have been so —

It was long, long ago,
And none living now can pretend to know.

But some Indians say
(Believe it who may)
That as over he went
In that dreadful descent,
Some power interposed with a kindly intent.
And, to save his poor bones,
Man, with wood- skin and freight, were all turned into
stones !

Rocks (the wood-skin and package) are now seen by all,

Who may visit that fall.
But where's the old man ? It is not quite so clear

That he doth appear.

" He's perhaps washed away.

Hyde, D.D._\n\nIn the first volume of Judge Fornander's elaborate work on \"The\nPolynesian Race\" he has given some old Hawaiian legends which closely\nresemble the Old Testament history. How shall we account for such\ncoincidences?\n\nTake, for instance, the Hawaiian account of the Creation. The\n_Kane_, _Ku_ and _Lono:_ or, Sunlight, Substance, and Sound,--these\nconstituted a triad named _Ku-Kaua-Kahi_, or the Fundamental Supreme\nUnity. In worship the reverence due was expressed by such epithets as\n_Hi-ka-po-loa, Oi-e,_ Most Excellent, etc. \"These gods existed from\neternity, from and before chaos, or, as the Hawaiian term expressed\nit, '_mai ka po mia_' (from the time of night, darkness, chaos). By\nan act of their will these gods dissipated or broke into pieces the\nexisting, surrounding, all-containing _po_, night, or chaos. By this\nact light entered into space. They then created the heavens, three in\nnumber, as a place to dwell in; and the earth to be their footstool,\n_he keehina honua a Kane_. Next they created the sun, moon, stars,\nand a host of angels, or spirits--_i kini akua_--to minister to\nthem. Last of all they created man as the model, or in the likeness\nof Kane. The body of the first man was made of red earth--_lepo ula_,\nor _alaea_--and the spittle of the gods--_wai nao_. His head was made\nof a whitish clay--_palolo_--which was brought from the four ends of\nthe world by Lono. When the earth-image of Kane was ready, the three\ngods breathed into its nose, and called on it to rise, and it became\na living being. Afterwards the first woman was created from one of\nthe ribs--_lalo puhaka_--of the man while asleep, and these two were\nthe progenitors of all mankind. They are called in the chants and in\nvarious legends by a large number of different names; but the most\ncommon for the man was Kumuhonua, and for the woman Keolakuhonua\n[or _Lalahonua_].\n\n\"Of the creation of animals these chants are silent; but from the\npure tradition it may be inferred that the earth at the time of its\ncreation or emergence from the watery chaos was stocked with vegetable\nand animal. The animals specially mentioned in the tradition as having\nbeen created by Kane were hogs (_puaa_), dogs (_ilio_), lizards or\nreptiles (_moo_).\n\n\"Another legend of the series, that of _Wela-ahi-lani_, states\nthat after Kane had destroyed the world by fire, on account of the\nwickedness of the people then living, he organized it as it now is,\nand created the first man and the first woman, with the assistance\nof Ku and Lono, nearly in the same manner as narrated in the former\nlegend of Kumuhonua. In this legend the man is called Wela-ahi-lani,\nand the woman is called Owe.\"\n\nOf the primeval home, the original ancestral seat of mankind,\nHawaiian traditions speak in highest praise. \"It had a number of\nnames of various meanings, though the most generally occurring,\nand said to be the oldest, was _Kalana-i-hau-ola_ (Kalana with\nthe life-giving dew). It was situated in a large country, or\ncontinent, variously called in the legends Kahiki-honua-kele,\nKahiki-ku, Kapa-kapa-ua-a-Kane, Molo-lani. Among other names\nfor the primary homestead, or paradise, are _Pali-uli_ (the blue\nmountain), _Aina-i-ka-kaupo-o-Kane_ (the land in the heart of Kane),\n_Aina-wai-akua-a-Kane_ (the land of the divine water of Kane). The\ntradition says of Pali-uli, that it was a sacred, tabooed land; that\na man must be righteous to attain it; if faulty or sinful he will not\nget there; if he looks behind he will not get there; if he prefers his\nfamily he will not enter Pali-uli.\" \"Among other adornments of the\nPolynesian Paradise, the Kalana-i-hau-ola, there grew the _Ulu kapu\na Kane_, the breadfruit tabooed for Kane, and the _ohia hemolele_,\nthe sacred apple-tree. The priests of the olden time are said to\nhave held that the tabooed fruits of these trees were in some manner\nconnected with the trouble and death of Kumuhonua and Lalahonua,\nthe first man and the first woman. Hence in the ancient chants he is\ncalled _Kane-laa-uli, Kumu-uli, Kulu-ipo_, the fallen chief, he who\nfell on account of the tree, or names of similar import.\""

  "passage_text": "According to those legends of Kumuhonua and Wela-ahi-lani, \"at the\ntime when the gods created the stars, they also created a multitude\nof angels, or spirits (_i kini akua_), who were not created like\nmen, but made from the spittle of the gods (_i kuhaia_), to be their\nservants or messengers. These spirits, or a number of them, disobeyed\nand revolted, because they were denied the _awa_; which means that\nthey were not permitted to be worshipped, _awa_ being a sacrificial\noffering and sign of worship. These evil spirits did not prevail,\nhowever, but were conquered by Kane, and thrust down into uttermost\ndarkness (_ilalo loa i ka po_). The chief of these spirits was called\nby some Kanaloa, by others Milu, the ruler of Po; Akua ino; Kupu ino,\nthe evil spirit. Other legends, however, state that the veritable and\nprimordial lord of the Hawaiian inferno was called Manua. The inferno\nitself bore a number of names, such as Po-pau-ole, Po-kua-kini,\nPo-kini-kini, Po-papa-ia-owa, Po-ia-milu. Milu, according to those\nother legends, was a chief of superior wickedness on earth who was\nthrust down into Po, but who was really both inferior and posterior to\nManua. This inferno, this Po, with many names, one of which remarkably\nenough was _Ke-po-lua-ahi_, the pit of fire, was not an entirely\ndark place. There was light of some kind and there was fire. The\nlegends further tell us that when Kane, Ku, and Lono were creating\nthe first man from the earth, Kanaloa was present, and in imitation\nof Kane, attempted to make another man out of the earth. When his\nclay model was ready, he called to it to become alive, but no life\ncame to it. Then Kanaloa became very angry, and said to Kane, 'I\nwill take your man, and he shall die,' and so it happened. Hence the\nfirst man got his other name _Kumu-uli_, which means a fallen chief,\n_he 'lii kahuli_.... With the Hawaiians, Kanaloa is the personified\nspirit of evil, the origin of death, the prince of Po, or chaos, and\nyet a revolted, disobedient spirit, who was conquered and punished by\nKane. The introduction and worship of Kanaloa, as one of the great\ngods in the Hawaiian group, can be traced back only to the time of\nthe immigration from the southern groups, some eight hundred years\nago. In the more ancient chants he is never mentioned in conjunction\nwith Kane, Ku, and Lono, and even in later Hawaiian mythology he never\ntook precedence of Kane. The Hawaiian legend states that the oldest\nson of Kumuhonua, the first man, was called Laka, and that the next\nwas called Ahu, and that Laka was a bad man; he killed his brother Ahu.\n\n\"There are these different Hawaiian genealogies, going back with\nmore or less agreement among themselves to the first created man. The\ngenealogy of Kumuhonua gives thirteen generations inclusive to Nuu,\nor Kahinalii, or the line of Laka, the oldest son of Kumuhonua. (The\nline of Seth from Adam to Noah counts ten generations.) The second\ngenealogy, called that of Kumu-uli, was of greatest authority among\nthe highest chiefs down to the latest times, and it was taboo to teach\nit to the common people. This genealogy counts fourteen generations\nfrom Huli-houna, the first man, to Nuu, or Nana-nuu, but inclusive,\non the line of Laka. The third genealogy, which, properly speaking,\nis that of Paao, the high-priest who came with Pili from Tahiti,\nabout twenty-five generations ago, and was a reformer of the Hawaiian\npriesthood, and among whose descendants it has been preserved, counts\nonly twelve generations from Kumuhonua to Nuu, on the line of Kapili,\nyoungest son of Kumuhonua.\""
}

  "passage_text": "\"In the Hawaiian group there are several legends of the Flood. One\nlegend relates that in the time of Nuu, or Nana-nuu (also pronounced\n_lana_, that is, floating), the flood, _Kaiakahinalii_, came upon\nthe earth, and destroyed all living beings; that Nuu, by command of\nhis god, built a large vessel with a house on top of it, which was\ncalled and is referred to in chants as '_He waa halau Alii o ka Moku_,'\nthe royal vessel, in which he and his family, consisting of his wife,\nLilinoe, his three sons and their wives, were saved. When the flood\nsubsided, Kane, Ku, and Lono entered the _waa halau_ of Nuu, and told\nhim to go out. He did so, and found himself on the top of Mauna Kea\n(the highest mountain on the island of Hawaii). He called a cave\nthere after the name of his wife, and the cave remains there to this\nday--as the legend says in testimony of the fact. Other versions of the\nlegend say that Nuu landed and dwelt in Kahiki-honua-kele, a large and\nextensive country.\" ... \"Nuu left the vessel in the evening of the day\nand took with him a pig, cocoanuts, and _awa_ as an offering to the\ngod Kane. As he looked up he saw the moon in the sky. He thought it\nwas the god, saying to himself, 'You are Kane, no doubt, though you\nhave transformed yourself to my sight.' So he worshipped the moon,\nand offered his offerings. Then Kane descended on the rainbow and\nspoke reprovingly to Nuu, but on account of the mistake Nuu escaped\npunishment, having asked pardon of Kane.\" ... \"Nuu's three sons were\nNalu-akea, Nalu-hoo-hua, and Nalu-mana-mana. In the tenth generation\nfrom Nuu arose Lua-nuu, or the second Nuu, known also in the legend\nas Kane-hoa-lani, Kupule, and other names. The legend adds that by\ncommand of his god he was the first to introduce circumcision to be\npractised among his descendants. He left his native home and moved a\nlong way off until he reached a land called Honua-ilalo, 'the southern\ncountry.' Hence he got the name Lalo-kona, and his wife was called\nHonua-po-ilalo. He was the father of Ku-nawao by his slave-woman Ahu\n(O-ahu) and of Kalani-menehune by his wife, Mee-hewa. Another says\nthat the god Kane ordered Lua-nuu to go up on a mountain and perform\na sacrifice there. Lua-nuu looked among the mountains of Kahiki-ku,\nbut none of them appeared suitable for the purpose. Then Lua-nuu\ninquired of God where he might find a proper place. God replied to\nhim: 'Go travel to the eastward, and where you find a sharp-peaked\nhill projecting precipitously into the ocean, that is the hill for\nthe sacrifice.' Then Lua-nuu and his son, Kupulu-pulu-a-Nuu, and his\nservant, Pili-lua-nuu, started off in their boat to the eastward. In\nremembrance of this event the Hawaiians called the back of Kualoa\n_Koo-lau_; Oahu (after one of Lua-nuu's names), _Kane-hoa-lani_;\nand the smaller hills in front of it were named _Kupu-pulu_ and\n_Pili-lua-nuu_. Lua-nuu is the tenth descendant from Nuu by both the\noldest and the youngest of Nuu's sons. This oldest son is represented\nto have been the progenitor of the _Kanaka-maoli_, the people living\non the mainland of Kane (_Aina kumupuaa a Kane_): the youngest was the\nprogenitor of the white people (_ka poe keo keo maoli_). This Lua-nuu\n(like Abraham, the tenth from Noah, also like Abraham), through his\ngrandson, Kini-lau-a-mano, became the ancestor of the twelve children\nof the latter, and the original founder of the Menehune people,\nfrom whom this legend makes the Polynesian family descend.\"\n\nThe Rev. Sheldon Dibble, in his history of the Sandwich Islands,\npublished at Lahainaluna, in 1843, gives a tradition which very\nmuch resembles the history of Joseph. \"Waikelenuiaiku was one of ten\nbrethren who had one sister. They were all the children of one father,\nwhose name was Waiku. Waikelenuiaiku was much beloved by his father,\nbut his brethren hated him. On account of their hatred they carried him\nand cast him into a pit belonging to Holonaeole. The oldest brother\nhad pity on him, and gave charge to Holonaeole to take good care of\nhim. Waikelenuiaiku escaped and fled to a country over which reigned a\nking whose name was Kamohoalii. There he was thrown into a dark place,\na pit under ground, in which many persons were confined for various\ncrimes. Whilst confined in this dark place he told his companions to\ndream dreams and tell them to him. The night following four of the\nprisoners had dreams. The first dreamed that he saw a ripe _ohia_\n(native apple), and his spirit ate it; the second dreamed that he saw\na ripe banana, and his spirit ate it; the third dreamed that he saw a\nhog, and his spirit ate it; and the fourth dreamed that he saw _awa_,\npressed out the juice, and his spirit drank it. The first three dreams,\npertaining to food, Waikelenuiaiku interpreted unfavorably, and told\nthe dreamers they must prepare to die. The fourth dream, pertaining to\ndrink, he interpreted to signify deliverance and life. The first three\ndreamers were slain according to the interpretation, and the fourth\nwas delivered and saved. Afterward this last dreamer told Kamohoalii,\nthe king of the land, how wonderful was the skill of Waikelenuiaiku in\ninterpreting dreams, and the king sent and delivered him from prison\nand made him a principal chief in his kingdom.\""

  "passage_text": "Judge Fornander alludes to this legend, giving the name,
however, _Aukelenui-a-Iku_, and adding to it the account of
the hero's journey to the place where the water of life was
kept (_ka-wai-ola-loa-a-Kane_), his obtaining it and therewith
resuscitating his brothers, who had been killed by drowning some
years before. Another striking similarity is that furnished to Judge
Fornander in the legend of _Ke-alii-waha-nui_: "He was king of the
country called Honua-i-lalo. He oppressed the Menehune people. Their
god Kane sent Kane-apua and Kaneloa, his elder brother, to bring the
people away, and take them to the land which Kane had given them, and
which was called _Ka aina momona a Kane_, or _Ka one lauena a Kane_,
and also _Ka aina i ka haupo a Kane_. The people were then told to
observe the four Ku days in the beginning of the month as _Kapu-hoano_
(sacred or holy days), in remembrance of this event, because they
thus arose (_Ku_) to depart from that land. Their offerings on the
occasion were swine and goats." The narrator of the legend explains
that formerly there were goats without horns, called _malailua_,
on the slopes of Mauna Loa on Hawaii, and that they were found there
up to the time of Kamehameha I. The legend further relates that after
leaving the land of Honualalo, the people came to the _Kai-ula-a-Kane_
(the Red Sea of Kane); that they were pursued by Ke-alii-waha-nui;
that Kane-apua and Kanaloa prayed to Lono, and finally reached the
_Aina lauena a Kane_.

"In the famous Hawaiian legend of _Hiiaka-i-ka-poli-o-Pele_, it
is said that when Hiiaka went to the island of Kauai to recover
and restore to life the body of Lohiau, the lover of her sister,
Pele, she arrived at the foot of the Kalalau Mountain shortly before
sunset. Being told by her friends at Haena that there would not be
daylight sufficient to climb the _pali_ (precipice) and get the body
out of the cave in which it was hidden, she prayed to her gods to keep
the sun stationary (_i ka muli o Hea_) over the brook Hea, until she
had accomplished her object. The prayer was heard, the mountain was
climbed, the guardians of the cave vanquished, and the body recovered."

A story of retarding the sun and making the day longer to accomplish
his purpose is told of Maui-a-kalana, according to Dibble's history.

Judge Fornander alludes to one other legend with incidents similar to
the Old Testament history wherein "Na-ula-a-Mainea, an Oahu prophet,
left Oahu for Kauai, was upset in his canoe, was swallowed by a whale,
and thrown up alive on the beach at Wailua, Kauai."

Judge Fornander says that, when he first heard the legend of the two
brother prophets delivering the Menehune people, "he was inclined to
doubt its genuineness and to consider it as a paraphrase or adaptation
of the Biblical account by some semi-civilized or semi-Christianized
Hawaiian, after the discovery of the group by Captain Cook. But a
larger and better acquaintance with Hawaiian folk-lore has shown that
though the details of the legend, as interpreted by the Christian
Hawaiian from whom it was received, may possibly in some degree, and
unconsciously to him, perhaps, have received a Biblical coloring, yet
the main facts of the legend, with the identical names of persons and
places, are referred to more or less distinctly in other legends of
undoubted antiquity." And the Rev. Mr. Dibble, in his history, says
of these Hawaiian legends, that "they were told to the missionaries
before the Bible was translated into the Hawaiian tongue, and before
the people knew much of sacred history. The native who acted as
assistant in translating the history of Joseph was forcibly struck
with its similarity to their ancient tradition. Neither is there
the least room for supposing that the songs referred to are recent
inventions. They can all be traced back for generations, and are
known by various persons residing on different islands who have had
no communication with each other. Some of them have their date in
the reign of some ancient king, and others have existed time out of
mind. It may also be added, that both their narrations and songs are
known the best by the very oldest of the people, and those who never
learned to read; whose education and training were under the ancient
system of heathenism."

"Two hypotheses," says Judge Fornander, "may with some plausibility be
suggested to account for this remarkable resemblance of folk-lore. One
is, that during the time of the Spanish galleon trade, in the sixteenth
and seventeenth centuries, between the Spanish Main and Manila,
some shipwrecked people, Spaniards and Portuguese, had obtained
sufficient influence to introduce these scraps of Bible history
into the legendary lore of this people.... On this fact hypothesis
I remark that, if the shipwrecked foreigners were educated men, or
only possessed of such Scriptural knowledge as was then imparted to
the commonality of laymen, it is morally impossible to conceive that
a Spaniard of the sixteenth century should confine his instruction to
some of the leading events of the Old Testament, and be totally silent
upon the Christian dispensation, and the cruciolatry, mariolatry,
and hagiolatry of that day. And it is equally impossible to conceive
that the Hawaiian listeners, chiefs, priests, or commoners, should have
retained and incorporated so much of the former in their own folk-lore,
and yet have utterly forgotten every item bearing upon the latter."
}

  "passage_text": ""The other hypothesis is, that at some remote period either a body
of the scattered Israelites had arrived at these islands direct, or
in Malaysia, before the exodus of 'the Polynesian family,' and thus
imparted a knowledge of their doctrines, of the early life of their
ancestors, and of some of their peculiar customs, and that having
been absorbed by the people among whom they found a refuge, this is
all that remains to attest their presence--intellectual tombstones
over a lost and forgotten race, yet sufficient after twenty-six
centuries of silence to solve in some measure the ethnic puzzle of
the lost tribes of Israel. In regard to this second hypothesis, it
is certainly more plausible and cannot be so curtly disposed of as
the Spanish theory.... So far from being copied one from the other,
they are in fact independent and original versions of a once common
legend, or series of legends, held alike by Cushite, Semite, Turanian,
and Aryan, up to a certain time, when the divergencies of national
life and other causes brought other subjects peculiar to each other
prominently in the foreground; and that as these divergencies hardened
into system and creed, that grand old heirloom of a common past became
overlaid and colored by the peculiar social and religious atmosphere
through which it has passed up to the surface of the present time. But
besides this general reason for refusing to adopt the Israelitish
theory, that the Polynesian legends were introduced by fugitive or
emigrant Hebrews from the subverted kingdoms of Israel or Judah,
there is the more special reason to be added that the organization
and splendor of Solomon's empire, his temple, and his wisdom became
proverbial among the nations of the East subsequent to his time;
on all these, the Polynesian legends are absolutely silent."

In commenting on the legend of _Hiiaka-i-ka-poli-o-Pele_, Judge
Fornander says: "If the Hebrew legend of Joshua or a Cushite version
give rise to it, it only brings down the community of legends a little
later in time. And so would the legend of _Naulu-a-Mahea_,... unless
the legend of Jonah, with which it corresponds in a measure, as well
as the previous legend of Joshua and the sun, were Hebrew anachronisms
compiled and adapted in later times from long antecedent materials,
of which the Polynesian references are but broken and distorted echoes,
bits of legendary mosaics, displaced from their original surroundings
and made to fit with later associations."

In regard to the account of the Creation, he remarks that "the Hebrew
legend infers that the god Elohim existed contemporaneously with
and apart from the chaos. The Hawaiian legend makes the three great
gods, Kane, Ku, and Lono, evolve themselves out of chaos.... The
order of creation, according to Hawaiian folk-lore, was that after
Heaven and earth had been separated, and the ocean had been stocked
with its animals, the stars were created, then the moon, then the
sun." Alluding to the fact that the account in Genesis is truer to
nature, Judge Fornander nevertheless propounds the inquiry whether
this fact may not "indicate that the Hebrew text is a later emendation
of an older but once common tradition"?

Highest antiquity is claimed for Hawaiian traditions in regard to
events subsequent to the creation of man. "In one of the sacrificial
hymns of the Marquesans, when human victims were offered, frequent
allusions were made to 'the red apples eaten in Naoau,' ... and to the
'tabooed apples of Atea,' as the cause of death, wars, pestilence,
famine, and other calamities, only to be averted or atoned for by the
sacrifice of human victims. The close connection between the Hawaiian
and the Marquesan legends indicates a common origin, and that origin
can be no other than that from which the Chaldean and Hebrew legends
of sacred trees, disobedience, and fall also sprang." In comparison of
"the Hawaiian myth of Kanaloa as a fallen angel antagonistic to the
great gods, as the spirit of evil and death in the world, the Hebrew
legends are more vague and indefinite as to the existence of an evil
principle. The serpent of Genesis, the Satan of Job, the Hillel of
Isaiah, the dragon of the Apocalypse--all point, however, to the
same underlying idea that the first cause of sin, death, evil, and
calamities, was to be found in disobedience and revolt from God. They
appear as disconnected scenes of a once grand drama that in olden
times riveted the attention of mankind, and of which, strange to
say, the clearest synopsis and the most coherent recollection are,
so far, to be found in Polynesian traditions. It is probably in vain
to inquire with whom the legend of an evil spirit and his operations
in Heaven and on earth had its origin. Notwithstanding the apparent
unity of design and remarkable coincidence in many points, yet the
differences in coloring, detail, and presentation are too great to
suppose the legend borrowed by one from either of the others. It
probably descended to the Chaldeans, Polynesians, and Hebrews alike,
from a source or people anterior to themselves, of whom history now
is silent."

II"
}

Forbes_\n\nI.--SNARING THE SUN\n\nMaui was the son of Hina-lau-ae and Hina, and they dwelt at a place\ncalled Makalia, above Kahakuloa, on West Maui. Now, his mother Hina\nmade _kapas_. And as she spread them out to dry, the days were so\nshort that she was put to great trouble and labor in hanging them\nout and taking them in day after day until they were dry. Maui,\nseeing this, was filled with pity for her, for the days were so\nshort that, no sooner had she got her kapas all spread out to dry,\nthan the Sun went down, and she had to take them in again. So he\ndetermined to make the Sun go slower. He first went to Wailohi, in\nHamakua, on East Maui, to observe the motions of the Sun. There he\nsaw that it rose toward Hana. He then went up on Haleakala, and saw\nthat the Sun in its course came directly over that mountain. He then\nwent home again, and after a few days went to a place called Paeloko,\nat Waihee. There he cut down all the cocoanut-trees, and gathered the\nfibre of the cocoanut husks in great quantity. This he manufactured\ninto strong cord. One Moemoe, seeing this, said tauntingly to him:\n\"Thou wilt never catch the Sun. Thou art an idle nobody.\"\n\nMaui answered: \"When I conquer my enemy, and my desire is attained,\nI will be your death.\" So he went up Haleakala again, taking his\ncord with him. And when the Sun arose above where he was stationed,\nhe prepared a noose of the cord and, casting it, snared one of the\nSun's larger beams and broke it off. And thus he snared and broke off,\none after another, all the strong rays of the Sun.\n\nThen shouted he exultingly: \"Thou art my captive, and now I will kill\nthee for thy going so swiftly.\"\n\nAnd the Sun said: \"Let me live, and thou shalt see me go more slowly\nhereafter. Behold, hast thou not broken off all my strong legs,\nand left me only the weak ones?\"\n\nSo the agreement was made, and Maui permitted the Sun to pursue\nits course, and from that time on it went more slowly; and that is\nthe reason why the days are longer at one season of the year than at\nanother. It was this that gave the name to that mountain, which should\nproperly be called _Alehe-ka-la_ (sun snarer), and not _Haleakala_.\n\nWhen Maui returned from this exploit, he went to find Moemoe, who\nhad reviled him. But that individual was not at home. He went on in\nhis pursuit till he came upon him at a place called Kawaiopilopilo,\non the shore to the eastward of the black rock called Kekaa, north\nof Lahaina. Moemoe dodged him up hill and down, until at last Maui,\ngrowing wroth, leaped upon and slew the fugitive. And the dead body\nwas transformed into a long rock, which is there to this day, by the\nside of the road."

These\nfour were fishermen. One morning, just as the edge of the Sun lifted\nitself up, Maui-mua roused his brethren to go fishing. So they\nlaunched their canoe from the beach at Kaupo, on the island of Maui,\nwhere they were dwelling, and proceeded to the fishing ground. Having\narrived there, they were beginning to fish, when Maui-o-ka-lana saw the\nlight of a fire on the shore they had left, and said to his brethren:\n\"Behold, there is a fire burning. Whose can this fire be?\"\n\nAnd they answered: \"Whose, indeed? Let us return to the shore, that\nwe may get our food cooked; but first let us get some fish.\"\n\nSo, after they had obtained some fish, they turned toward the shore;\nand when the canoe touched the beach Maui-mua leaped ashore and ran\ntoward the spot where the fire had been burning. Maui-mua was\ndefeated, and returned to the house to his brethren.\n\nThen said they to him: \"How about the fire?\"\n\n\"How, indeed?\" he answered. \"When I got there, behold, there was\nno fire; it was out. I supposed some man had the fire, and behold,\nit was not so; the alae are the proprietors of the fire, and our\nbananas are all stolen.\"\n\nWhen they heard that, they were filled with anger, and decided not\nto go fishing again, but to wait for the next appearance of the\nfire. But after many days had passed without their seeing the fire,\nthey went fishing again, and behold, there was the fire! And so they\nwere continually tantalized. Only when they were out fishing would\nthe fire appear, and when they returned they could not find it.\n\nThis was the way of it. The curly-tailed alae knew that Maui and\nHina had only these four sons, and if any of them stayed on shore\nto watch the fire while the others were out in the canoe the alae\nknew it by counting those in the canoe, and would not light the\nfire. Only when they could count four men in the canoe would they\nlight the fire. So Maui-mua thought it over, and said to his brethren:\n\"To-morrow morning do you go fishing, and I will stay ashore. But do\nyou take the calabash and dress it in kapa, and put it in my place\nin the canoe, and then go out to fish.\"\n\nThey did so, and when they went out to fish the next morning, the alae\ncounted and saw four figures in the canoe, and then they lit the fire\nand put the bananas on to roast. Before they were fully baked one of\nthe alae cried out: \"Our dish is cooked! Behold, Hina has a smart son.\"\n\nAnd with that, Maui-mua, who had stolen close to them unperceived,\nleaped forward, seized the curly-tailed alae and exclaimed: \"Now\nI will kill you, you scamp of an alae! Behold, it is you who are\nkeeping the fire from us. I will be the death of you for this.\"\n\nThen answered the alae: \"If you kill me the secret dies with me,\nand you won't get the fire.\" As Maui-mua began to wring its neck, the\nalae again spoke, and said: \"Let me live, and you shall have the fire.\"\n\nSo Maui-mua said: \"Tell me, where is the fire?\"\n\nThe alae replied: \"It is in the leaf of the a-pe plant\" (_Alocasia\nmacrorrhiza_).\n\nSo, by the direction of the alae, Maui-mua began to rub the leaf-stalk\nof the a-pe plant with a piece of stick, but the fire would not\ncome. Again he asked: \"Where is this fire that you are hiding from me?\"\n\nThe alae answered: \"In a green stick.\"\n\nAnd he rubbed a green stick, but got no fire. So it went on, until\nfinally the alae told him he would find it in a dry stick; and so,\nindeed, he did. Forbes_\n\nAll volcanic phenomena are associated in Hawaiian legendary lore\nwith the goddess Pele; and it is a somewhat curious fact that to\nthe same celebrated personage is also attributed a great flood that\noccurred in ancient times. The legends of this flood are various,\nbut mainly connected with the doings of Pele in this part of the\nPacific Ocean. The story runs thus:\n\nKahinalii was the mother of Pele; Kanehoalani was her father; and\nher two brothers were Kamohoalii and Kahuilaokalani. Pele was born\nin the land of Hapakuela, a far-distant land at the edge of the sky,\ntoward the southwest. There she lived with her parents until she was\ngrown up, when she married Wahialoa; and to these were born a daughter\nnamed Laka, and a son named Menehune. But after a time Pele's husband,\nWahialoa, was enticed away from her by Pele-kumulani. The deserted\nPele, being much displeased and troubled in mind on account of her\nhusband, started on her travels in search of him, and came in the\ndirection of the Hawaiian Islands. Now, at that time these islands were\na vast waste. There was no sea, nor was there any fresh water. When\nPele set out on her journey, her parents gave her the sea to go with\nher and bear her canoes onward. So she sailed forward, flood-borne by\nthe sea, until she reached the land of Pakuela, and thence onward to\nthe land of Kanaloa. From her head she poured forth the sea as she\nwent, and her brothers composed the celebrated ancient mele:\n\n    O the sea, the great sea!\n    Forth bursts the sea:\n    Behold, it bursts on Kanaloa!\n\nBut the waters of the sea continued to rise until only the highest\npoints of the great mountains, Haleakala, Maunakea, and Maunaloa,\nwere visible; all else was covered. Afterward the sea receded until it\nreached its present level. This event is called the _Kai a Kahinalii_\n(Sea of Kahinalii), because it was from Kahinalii, her mother, that\nPele received the gift of the sea, and she herself only brought it\nto Hawaii.\n\nAnd from that time to this, Pele and all her family forsook their\nformer land of Hapakuela and have dwelt in Hawaii-nei, Pele coming\nfirst and the rest following at a later time.\n\nOn her first arrival at Hawaii-nei, Pele dwelt on the island of\nKauai. From there she went to Kalaupapa, [1] on the island of\nMolokai, and dwelt in the crater of Kauhako at that place; thence\nshe departed to Puulaina, [2] near Lahainaluna, where she dug out\nthat crater. Afterward she moved still further to Haleakala, where\nshe stayed until she hollowed out that great crater; and finally she\nsettled at Kilauea, on the island of Hawaii, where she has remained\never since. [3]\n\nIV"
}

  "passage_text": "PELE AND KAHAWALI\n\n_From Ellis's \"Tour of Hawaii\"_\n\nIn the reign of Kealiikukii, an ancient king of Hawaii, Kahawali,\nchief of Puna, and one of his favorite companions went one day to\namuse themselves with the _holua_ (sled), on the sloping side of a\nhill, which is still called _ka holua ana o Kahawali_ (Kahawali's\nsliding-place). Vast numbers of the people gathered at the bottom of\nthe hill to witness the game, and a company of musicians and dancers\nrepaired thither to add to the amusement of the spectators. The\nperformers began their dance, and amidst the sound of drums and the\nsongs of the musicians the sledding of Kahawali and his companion\ncommenced. The hilarity of the occasion attracted the attention of\nPele, the goddess of the volcano, who came down from Kilauea to witness\nthe sport. Standing on the summit of the hill in the form of a woman,\nshe challenged Kahawali to slide with her. He accepted the offer,\nand they set off together down the hill. Pele, less acquainted with\nthe art of balancing herself on the narrow sled than her rival, was\nbeaten, and Kahawali was applauded by the spectators as he returned\nup the side of the hill.\n\nBefore starting again, Pele asked him to give her his _papa holua_,\nbut he, supposing from her appearance that she was no more than a\nnative woman, said: \"_Aole!_ (no!) Are you my wife, that you should\nobtain my sled?\" And, as if impatient at being delayed, he adjusted his\npapa, ran a few yards to take a spring, and then, with this momentum\nand all his strength he threw himself upon it and shot down the hill.\n\nPele, incensed at his answer, stamped her foot on the ground and\nan earthquake followed, which rent the hill in sunder. She called,\nand fire and liquid lava arose, and, assuming her supernatural form,\nwith these irresistible ministers of vengeance, she followed down\nthe hill. When Kahawali reached the bottom, he arose, and on looking\nbehind saw Pele, accompanied by thunder and lightning, earthquake, and\nstreams of burning lava, closely pursuing him. He took up his broad\nspear which he had stuck in the ground at the beginning of the game,\nand, accompanied by his friend, fled for his life. The musicians,\ndancers, and crowds of spectators were instantly overwhelmed by the\nfiery torrent, which, bearing on its foremost wave the enraged goddess,\ncontinued to pursue Kahawali and his companion. They ran till they\ncame to an eminence called Puukea. Here Kahawali threw off his cloak\nof netted ki leaves and proceeded toward his house, which stood near\nthe shore. He met his favorite pig and saluted it by touching noses,\nthen ran to the house of his mother, who lived at Kukii, saluted her by\ntouching noses, and said: \"_Aloha ino oe, eia ihonei paha oe e make ai,\nke ai mainei Pele._\" (Compassion great to you! Close here, perhaps,\nis your death; Pele comes devouring.) Leaving her, he met his wife,\nKanakawahine, and saluted her. The burning torrent approached, and she\nsaid: \"Stay with me here, and let us die together.\" He said: \"No; I go,\nI go.\" He then saluted his two children, Poupoulu and Kaohe, and said,\n\"_Ke ue nei au ia olua_.\" (I grieve for you two.) The lava rolled near,\nand he ran till a deep chasm arrested his progress. He laid down his\nspear and walked over on it in safety. His friend called out for his\nhelp; he held out his spear over the chasm; his companion took hold of\nit and he drew him securely over. By this time Pele was coming down\nthe chasm with accelerated motion. He ran till he reached Kula. Here\nhe met his sister, Koai, but had only time to say, _\"Aloha oe!\"_\n(Alas for you!) and then ran on to the shore. His younger brother had\njust landed from his fishing-canoe, and had hastened to his house to\nprovide for the safety of his family, when Kahawali arrived. He and\nhis friend leaped into the canoe, and with his broad spear paddled\nout to sea. Pele, perceiving his escape, ran to the shore and hurled\nafter him, with prodigious force, great stones and fragments of rock,\nwhich fell thickly around but did not strike his canoe. When he had\npaddled a short distance from the shore the _kumukahi_ (east wind)\nsprung up. He fixed his broad spear upright in the canoe, that it\nmight answer the double purpose of mast and sail, and by its aid he\nsoon reached the island of Maui, where they rested one night and then\nproceeded to Lanai. The day following they moved on to Molokai, thence\nto Oahu, the abode of Kolonohailaau, his father, and Kanewahinekeaho,\nhis sister, to whom he related his disastrous perils, and with whom\nhe took up his permanent abode.\n\nV"

  "passage_text": "HIKU AND KAWELU

_J. S. Emerson_

Not far from the summit of Hualalai, on the island of Hawaii, in
the cave on the southern side of the ridge, lived Hina and her son,
the _kupua_, or demigod, Hiku. All his life long as a child and a
youth, Hiku had lived alone with his mother on this mountain summit,
and had never once been permitted to descend to the plains below to
see the abodes of men and to learn of their ways. From time to time,
his quick ear had caught the sound of the distant _hula_ (drum) and
the voices of the gay merrymakers. Often had he wished to see the
fair forms of those who danced and sang in those far-off cocoanut
groves. But his mother, more experienced in the ways of the world,
had never given her consent. Now, at length, he felt that he was a
man, and as the sounds of mirth arose on his ears, again he asked
his mother to let him go for himself and mingle with the people
on the shore. His mother, seeing that his mind was made up to go,
reluctantly gave her consent and warned him not to stay too long,
but to return in good time. So, taking in his hand his faithful arrow,
_Pua Ne_, which he always carried, he started off.

This arrow was a sort of talisman, possessed of marvellous powers,
among which were the ability to answer his call and by its flight to
direct his journey.

Thus he descended over the rough clinker lava and through the groves of
koa that cover the southwestern flank of the mountain, until, nearing
its base, he stood on a distant hill; and consulting his arrow, he shot
it far into the air, watching its bird-like flight until it struck
on a distant hill above Kailua. To this hill he rapidly directed his
steps, and, picking up his arrow in due time, he again shot it into the
air. The second flight landed the arrow near the coast of Holualoa,
some six or eight miles south of Kailua. It struck on a barren waste
of _pahoehoe_, or lava rock, beside the waterhole of _Waikalai_,
known also as the _Wai a Hiku_ (Water of Hiku), where to this day all
the people of that vicinity go to get their water for man and beast.

Here he quenched his thirst, and nearing the village of Holualoa, again
shot the arrow, which, instinct with life, entered the courtyard of
the _alii_ or chief, of Kona, and from among the women who were there
singled out the fair princess Kawelu, and landed at her feet. Seeing
the noble bearing of Hiku as he approached to claim his arrow, she
stealthily hid it and challenged him to find it. Then Hiku called
to the arrow, "_Pua ne! Pua ne!_" and the arrow replied, "_Ne!_"
thus revealing its hiding-place.

This exploit with the arrow and the remarkable grace and personal
beauty of the young man quite won the heart of the princess, and she
was soon possessed by a strong passion for him, and determined to
make him her husband.

With her wily arts she detained him for several days at her home,
and when at last he was about to start for the mountain, she shut
him up in the house and thus detained him by force. But the words
of his mother, warning him not to remain too long, came to his mind,
and he determined to break away from his prison. So he climbed up to
the roof, and removing a portion of the thatch, made his escape.

When his flight was discovered by Kawelu, the infatuated girl was
distracted with grief. Refusing to be comforted, she tasted no food,
and ere many days had passed was quite dead. Messengers were despatched
who brought back the unhappy Hiku, author of all this sorrow. Bitterly
he wept over the corpse of his beloved, but it was now too late; the
spirit had departed to the nether world, ruled over by Milu. And now,
stung by the reproaches of her kindred and friends for his desertion,
and urged on by his real love for the fair one, he resolved to attempt
the perilous descent into the nether world and, if possible, to bring
her spirit back.

With the assistance of her friends, he collected from the mountain
slope a great quantity of the _kowali_, or convolvulus vine. He also
prepared a hollow cocoanut shell, splitting it into two closely fitting
parts. Then anointing himself with a mixture of rancid cocoanut and
kukui oil, which gave him a very strong corpse-like odor, he started
with his companions in the well-loaded canoes for a point in the sea
where the sky comes down to meet the water.

Arrived at the spot, he directed his comrades to lower him into the
abyss called by the Hawaiians the _Lua o Milu_. Taking with him his
cocoanut-shell and seating himself astride of the cross-stick of the
swing, or kowali, he was quickly lowered down by the long rope of
kowali vines held by his friends in the canoe above.

Soon he entered the great cavern where the shades of the departed were
gathered together. As he came among them, their curiosity was aroused
to learn who he was. And he heard many remarks, such as "Whew! what
an odor this corpse emits!" "He must have been long dead." He had
rather overdone the matter of the rancid oil. Even Milu himself,
as he sat on the bank watching the crowd, was completely deceived by
the stratagem, for otherwise he never would have permitted this bold
descent of a living man into his gloomy abode."

  "passage_text": "LOCATION OF THE LUA O MILU\n\nIn the myth of Hiku and Kawelu, the entrance to the Lua o Milu\nis placed out to sea opposite Holualoa and a few miles south of\nKailua. But the more usual account of the natives is, that it was\nsituated at the mouth of the great valley of Waipio, in a place called\nKeoni, where the sands have long since covered up and concealed from\nview this passage from the upper to the nether world.\n\nEvery year, so it is told, the procession of ghosts called by the\nnatives _Oio_, marches in solemn state down the Mahiki road, and at\nthis point enters the Lua o Milu. A man, recently living in Waimea,\nof the best reputation for veracity, stated that about thirty or more\nyears ago, he actually saw this ghostly company. He was walking up this\nroad in the evening, when he saw at a distance the _Oio_ appear, and\nknowing that should they encounter him his death would be inevitable,\nhe discreetly hid himself behind a tree and, trembling with fear, gazed\nin silence at the dread spectacle. There was Kamehameha, the conqueror,\nwith all his chiefs and warriors in military array, thousands of heroes\nwho had won renown in the olden time. Though all were silent as the\ngrave, they kept perfect step as they marched along, and passing\nthrough the woods down to Waipio, disappeared from his view.\n\nIn connection with the foregoing, Professor W. D. Alexander kindly\ncontributes the following:\n\n\"The valley of Waipio is a place frequently celebrated in the songs\nand traditions of Hawaii, as having been the abode of Akea and Milu,\nthe first kings of the island....\n\n\"Some said that the souls of the departed went to the _Po_ (place\nof night), and were annihilated or eaten by the gods there. Others\nsaid that some went to the regions of Akea and Milu. Akea (Wakea),\nthey said, was the first king of Hawaii. At the expiration of his\nreign, which terminated with his life at Waipio, where we then were,\nhe descended to a region far below, called Kapapahanaumoku (the island\nbearing rock or stratum), and founded a kingdom there. Milu, who was\nhis successor, and reigned in Hamakua, descended, when he died, to\nAkea and shared the government of the place with him. Their land is\na place of darkness; their food lizards and butterflies. There are\nseveral streams of water, of which they drink, and some said that\nthere were large kahilis and wide-spreading kou trees, beneath which\nthey reclined.\" [4]\n\n\"They had some very indistinct notion of a future state of happiness\nand of misery. They said that, after death, the ghost went first to\nthe region of Wakea, the name of their first reputed progenitor, and\nif it had observed the religious rites and ceremonies, was entertained\nand allowed to remain there. That was a place of houses, comforts,\nand pleasures. If the soul had failed to be religious, it found no\none there to entertain it, and was forced to take a desperate leap\ninto a place of misery below, called Milu.\n\n\"There were several precipices, from the verge of which the unhappy\nghosts were supposed to take the leap into the region of woe; three in\nparticular, one at the northern extremity of Hawaii, one at the western\ntermination of Maui, and the third at the northern point of Oahu.\" [5]\n\nNear the northwest point of Oahu is a rock called Leina Kauhane, where\nthe souls of the dead descended into Hades. In New Zealand the same\nterm, \"Reinga\" (the leaping place), is applied to the North Cape. The\nMarquesans have a similar belief in regard to the northermost island\nof their group, and apply the same term, \"Reinga,\" to their Avernus.\n\nVI"
}

  "passage_text": "LONOPUHA; OR, ORIGIN OF THE ART OF HEALING IN HAWAII

_Translated by Thos. G. Thrum_

During the time that Milu was residing at Waipio, Hawaii, the year
of which is unknown, there came to these shores a number of people,
with their wives, from that vague foreign land, Kahiki. But they were
all of godly kind (_ano akua nae_), it is said, and drew attention
as they journeyed from place to place. They arrived first at Niihau,
and from there they travelled through all the islands. At Hawaii
they landed at the south side, thence to Puna, Hilo, and settled at
Kukuihaele, Hamakua, just above Waipio.

On every island they visited there appeared various diseases, and
many deaths resulted, so that it was said this was their doings,
among the chiefs and people. The diseases that followed in their
train were chills, fevers, headache, _pani_, and so on.

These are the names of some of these people: Kaalaenuiahina,
Kahuilaokalani, Kaneikaulanaula, besides others. They brought
death, but one Kamakanuiahailono followed after them with healing
powers. This was perhaps the origin of sickness and the art of healing
with medicines in Hawaii.

As has been said, diseases settled on the different islands like an
epidemic, and the practice of medicine ensued, for Kamakanuiahailono
followed them in their journeyings. He arrived at Kau, stopping at
Kiolakaa, on the west side of Waiohinu, where a great multitude of
people were residing, and Lono was their chief. The stranger sat on a
certain hill, where many of the people visited him, for the reason that
he was a newcomer, a custom that is continued to this day. While there
he noticed the redness of skin of a certain one of them, and remarked,
"Oh, the redness of skin of that man!"

The people replied, "Oh, that is Lono, the chief of this land, and
he is a farmer."

He again spoke, asserting that his sickness was very great; for
through the redness of the skin he knew him to be a sick man.

They again replied that he was a healthy man, "but you consider him
very sick." He then left the residents and set out on his journey.

Some of those who heard his remarks ran and told the chief the
strange words, "that he was a very sick man." On hearing this,
Lono raised up his _oo_ (digger) and said, "Here I am, without any
sign of disease, and yet I am sick." And as he brought down his _oo_
with considerable force, it struck his foot and pierced it through,
causing the blood to flow freely, so that he fell and fainted away. At
this, one of the men seized a pig and ran after the stranger, who,
hearing the pig squealing, looked behind him and saw the man running
with it; and as he neared him he dropped it before him, and told him
of Lono's misfortune, Kamakanuiahailono then returned, gathering on
the way the young popolo seeds and its tender leaves in his garment
(_kihei_). When he arrived at the place where the wounded man was
lying he asked for some salt, which he took and pounded together with
the popolo and placed it with a cocoanut covering on the wound. From
then till night the flowing of the blood ceased. After two or three
weeks had elapsed he again took his departure.

While he was leisurely journeying, some one breathing heavily
approached him in the rear, and, turning around, there was the chief,
and he asked him: "What is it, Lono, and where are you going?"

Lono replied, "You healed me; therefore, as soon as you had departed I
immediately consulted with my successors, and have resigned my offices
to them, so that they will have control over all. As for myself,
I followed after you, that you might teach me the art of healing."

The _kahuna lapaau_ (medical priest) then said, "Open your mouth." When
Lono opened his mouth, the kahuna spat into it, [6] by which he
would become proficient in the calling he had chosen, and in which
he eventually became, in fact, very skilful.

As they travelled, he instructed Lono (on account of the accident
to his foot he was called Lonopuha) in the various diseases, and the
different medicines for the proper treatment of each. They journeyed
through Kau, Puna, and Hilo, thence onward to Hamakua as far as
Kukuihaele. Prior to their arrival there, Kamakanuiahailono said
to Lonopuha, "It is better that we reside apart, lest your healing
practice do not succeed; but you settle elsewhere, so as to gain
recognition from your own skill."

For this reason, Lonopuha went on farther and located in Waimanu,
and there practised the art of healing. On account of his labors here,
he became famous as a skilful healer, which fame Kamakanuiahailono and
others heard of at Kukuihaele; but he never revealed to _Kaalaenuiahina
ma_ (company) of his teaching of Lonopuha, through which he became
celebrated. It so happened that _Kaalaenuiahina ma_ were seeking an
occasion to cause Milu's death, and he was becoming sickly through
their evil efforts.

When Milu heard of the fame of Lonopuha as a skilful healer, because
of those who were afflicted with disease and would have died but for
his treatment, he sent his messenger after him. On arriving at Milu's
house, Lonopuha examined and felt of him, and then said, "You will
have no sickness, provided you be obedient to my teachings." He then
exercised his art, and under his medical treatment Milu recovered.

Lonopuha then said to him: "I have treated you, and you are well of
the internal ailments you suffered under, and only that from without
remains. Now, you must build a house of leaves and dwell therein in
quietness for a few weeks, to recuperate." These houses are called
_pipipi_, such being the place to which invalids are moved for
convalescent treatment unless something unforeseen should occur."

  "passage_text": "Upon Milu's removal thereto, Lonopuha advised him as follows: "O
King! you are to dwell in this house according to the length of time
directed, in perfect quietness; and should the excitement of sports
with attendant loud cheering prevail here, I warn you against these
as omens of evil for your death; and I advise you not to loosen the
_ti_ leaves of your house to peep out to see the cause, for on the
very day you do so, that day you will perish."

Some two weeks had scarcely passed since the King had been confined
in accordance with the kahuna's instructions, when noises from
various directions in proximity to the King's dwelling were heard,
but he regarded the advice of the priest all that day. The cause of
the commotion was the appearance of two birds playing in the air,
which so excited the people that they kept cheering them all that day.

Three weeks had almost passed when loud cheering was again heard in
Waipio, caused by a large bird decorated with very beautiful feathers,
which flew out from the clouds and soared proudly over the _palis_
(precipices) of Koaekea and Kaholokuaiwa, and poised gracefully
over the people; therefore, they cheered as they pursued it here and
there. Milu was much worried thereby, and became so impatient that
he could no longer regard the priest's caution; so he lifted some of
the ti leaves of his house to look out at the bird, when instantly
it made a thrust at him, striking him under the armpit, whereby his
life was taken and he was dead (_lilo ai kona ola a make iho la_).

The priest saw the bird flying with the liver of Milu; therefore, he
followed after it. When it saw that it was pursued, it immediately
entered into a sunken rock just above the base of the precipice of
Koaekea. As he reached the place, the blood was spattered around
where the bird had entered. Taking a piece of garment (_pahoola_), he
soaked it with the blood and returned and placed it in the opening in
the body of the dead King and poured healing medicine on the wound,
whereby Milu recovered. And the place where the bird entered with
Milu's liver has ever since been called Keakeomilu (the liver of Milu).

A long while afterward, when this death of the King was as nothing
(_i mea ole_), and he recovered as formerly, the priest refrained
not from warning him, saying: "You have escaped from this death;
there remains for you one other."

After Milu became convalescent from his recent serious experience,
a few months perhaps had elapsed, when the surf at Waipio became very
high and was breaking heavily on the beach. This naturally caused
much commotion and excitement among the people, as the numerous
surf-riders, participating in the sport, would land upon the beach
on their surf-boards. Continuous cheering prevailed, and the hilarity
rendered Milu so impatient at the restraint put upon him by the priest
that he forsook his wise counsel and joined in the exhilarating sport.

Seizing a surf-board he swam out some distance to the selected spot
for suitable surfs. Here he let the first and second combers pass
him; but watching his opportunity he started with the momentum of the
heavier third comber, catching the crest just right. Quartering on
the rear of his board, he rode in with majestic swiftness, and landed
nicely on the beach amid the cheers and shouts of the people. He then
repeated the venture and was riding in as successfully, when, in a
moment of careless abandon, at the place where the surfs finish as
they break on the beach, he was thrust under and suddenly disappeared,
while the surf-board flew from under and was thrown violently upon the
shore. The people in amazement beheld the event, and wildly exclaimed:
"Alas! Milu is dead! Milu is dead!" With sad wonderment they searched
and watched in vain for his body. Thus was seen the result of repeated
disobedience.

VII

A VISIT TO THE SPIRIT LAND; OR, THE STRANGE EXPERIENCE OF A WOMAN IN
KONA, HAWAII

_Mrs. E. N. Haley_

Kalima had been sick for many weeks, and at last died. Her friends
gathered around her with loud cries of grief, and with many expressions
of affection and sorrow at their loss they prepared her body for
its burial.

The grave was dug, and when everything was ready for the last rites
and sad act, husband and friends came to take a final look at the rigid
form and ashen face before it was laid away forever in the ground. The
old mother sat on the mat-covered ground beside her child, brushing
away the intrusive flies with a piece of cocoanut-leaf, and wiping
away the tears that slowly rolled down her cheeks. Now and then she
would break into a low, heart-rending wail, and tell in a sob-choked,
broken voice, how good this her child had always been to her, how her
husband loved her, and how her children would never have any one to
take her place. "Oh, why," she cried, "did the gods leave me? I am old
and heavy with years; my back is bent and my eyes are getting dark. I
cannot work, and am too old and weak to enjoy fishing in the sea,
or dancing and feasting under the trees. But this my child loved all
these things, and was so happy. Why is she taken and I, so useless,
left?" And again that mournful, sob-choked wail broke on the still
air, and was borne out to the friends gathered under the trees before
the door, and was taken up and repeated until the hardest heart would
have softened and melted at the sound. As they sat around on the mats
looking at their dead and listening to the old mother, suddenly Kalima
moved, took a long breath, and opened her eyes. They were frightened
at the miracle, but so happy to have her back again among them.

The old mother raised her hands and eyes to heaven and, with rapt
faith on her brown, wrinkled face, exclaimed: "The gods have let her
come back! How they must love her!"

Mother, husband, and friends gathered around and rubbed her hands
and feet, and did what they could for her comfort. In a few minutes
she revived enough to say, "I have something strange to tell you.""
}

  "passage_text": "Several days passed before she was strong enough to say more; then\ncalling her relatives and friends about her, she told them the\nfollowing weird and strange story:\n\n\"I died, as you know. I seemed to leave my body and stand beside it,\nlooking down on what _was_ me. The me that was standing there looked\nlike the form I was looking at, only, I was alive and the other was\ndead. I gazed at my body for a few minutes, then turned and walked\naway. I left the house and village, and walked on and on to the next\nvillage, and there I found crowds of people,--Oh, so many people! The\nplace which I knew as a small village of a few houses was a very\nlarge place, with hundreds of houses and thousands of men, women,\nand children. Some of them I knew and they spoke to me,--although\nthat seemed strange, for I knew they were dead,--but nearly all were\nstrangers. They were all so happy! They seemed not to have a care;\nnothing to trouble them. Joy was in every face, and happy laughter\nand bright, loving words were on every tongue.\n\n\"I left that village and walked on to the next. I was not tired, for\nit seemed no trouble to walk. It was the same there; thousands of\npeople, and every one so joyous and happy. Some of these I knew. I\nspoke to a few people, then went on again. I seemed to be on my way\nto the volcano,--to Pele's pit,--and could not stop, much as I wanted\nto do so.\n\n\"All along the road were houses and people, where I had never known\nany one to live. Every bit of good ground had many houses, and many,\nmany happy people on it. I felt so full of joy, too, that my heart\nsang within me, and I was glad to be dead.\n\n\"In time I came to South Point, and there, too, was a great crowd\nof people. The barren point was a great village, I was greeted with\nhappy _alohas_, then passed on. All through Kau it was the same, and\nI felt happier every minute. At last I reached the volcano. There\nwere some people there, but not so many as at other places. They,\ntoo, were happy like the others, but they said, 'You must go back to\nyour body. You are not to die yet.'\n\n\"I did not want to go back. I begged and prayed to be allowed to stay\nwith them, but they said, 'No, you must go back; and if you do not\ngo willingly, we will make you go.'\n\n\"I cried and tried to stay, but they drove me back, even beating me\nwhen I stopped and would not go on. So I was driven over the road\nI had come, back through all those happy people. They were still\njoyous and happy, but when they saw that I was not allowed to stay,\nthey turned on me and helped drive me, too.\n\n\"Over the sixty miles I went, weeping, followed by those cruel people,\ntill I reached my home and stood by my body again. I looked at it and\nhated it. Was that my body? What a horrid, loathsome thing it was to\nme now, since I had seen so many beautiful, happy creatures! Must I go\nand live in that thing again? No, I would not go into it; I rebelled\nand cried for mercy.\n\n\"'You must go into it; we will make you!' said my tormentors. They\ntook me and pushed me head foremost into the big toe.\n\n\"I struggled and fought, but could not help myself. They pushed and\nbeat me again, when I tried for the last time to escape. When I passed\nthe waist, I seemed to know it was of no use to struggle any more,\nso went the rest of the way myself. Then my body came to life again,\nand I opened my eyes.\n\n\"But I wish I could have stayed with those happy people. It was cruel\nto make me come back. My other body was so beautiful, and I was so\nhappy, so happy!\"\n\nVIII"
}
